Depression is a joy sucker. It takes every insecurity and everything that isn't right in your life and magnifies it to a point where it seems like nothing but a great big disappointment. And not being in a relationship, when it seems like everyone around you is getting married, takes being alone and turns it into loneliness. The worst thing about depression is the inability to remember ever having been happy. Which then makes the downward spiral feel inevitable. Time for introspection is healthy. But when you find yourself unable to do anything but stew and feel like a failure, you need to get out of your head and realize that this isn't the time to take your own inventory.

I wish there were some magical solution. Something I could say that would lift that feeling of failure and despair. But depression is like looking at the world through shit covered glasses. It does get better. Like a kaleidoscope, sometimes a simple move will change everything. Stay active. Make the effort to hang out with friends, even when you don't feel like it. Find things to do that don't require a lot of thinking, just doing. And keep talking to people, here, there and everywhere until you hear words that make sense to you.

I can definitely relate to this. I also had severe depression at 23 (and still do) and it was really tough seeing everyone around me getting married, having kids, buying cars and houses, going on fancy vacations... all that "grown up" stuff.

Looking back, I see that most of the people I knew who got married young either got divorced soon after, or are stuck in a miserable, loveless marriage after less than a decade. It's much better to take the time and find the right person to have a long-term relationship with, than to just jump into a relationship with the first person who comes along because you're lonely. I was guilty of this too when I was younger, and looking back on it, I'm glad I didn't rush into marriage with any of my exes because although they were generally nice people, we weren't right for each other. It's extremely important to find someone with the same values as you when it comes to the important things like work ethic, finances, parenting style (if you want kids) etc.

An important piece of advice I can give you is to stay off social media. People tend to post only their best moments to social media to make their lives seem spectacular, when in reality they're incredibly mundane. We're all guilty of doing this - we edit our social media presence to make our lives seem ideal - but for some reason, we forget that other people are doing this too. There are actually studies linking social media usage with mental illness, including depression. Now I'll admit, I still have a Facebook and an Instagram account, but I mainly use them to keep in touch with people I probably wouldn't otherwise. I don't mindlessly scroll through my newsfeed anymore looking at other people's photos, and I've honestly noticed that I've been less depressed since I stopped looking.

Another thing to keep in mind is that all the stuff people might brag about on social media (new car, expensive vacation, designer purse, etc) isn't necessarily paid for. A lot of people will buy things with money they don't have (using credit) just so they can make themselves feel better than everyone else. But in reality, their credit is a mess and they're one mishap away from having that fancy car repossessed or their house foreclosed upon. Don't get caught up in the mentality that things = success. Success is whatever you define it to be, and your success won't necessarily look like someone else's.

I hope this was helpful. If you'd like to chat more, don't be afraid to send me a PM (:

my family joined the local Y, and i may be becoming a bit of a gym rat. i’ve been doing a lot of group fitness classes and i’ve got meetings arranged with a personal trainer. it’s getting to be less excruciating and more enjoyable, and if anybody has tips for newbies feel free to reply below because i’m really quite new to this lol (most of my getting in shape has been through diet)

Stick with the group classes if you like them. Otherwise Meet with a trainer for a few times to learn form on deadlifts, squats; any compound movement. Take it slow and work up.

Make sure you take some branch chain amino acids in your water to encourage that muscle to develop. Eat a protein meal after-typically you want 0.7-1g of protein per pound to gain a bit of mass. Specific examples of that you can easily find online (e.g. chicken breast is about 35g of protein but obv serving size matters).

Make sure you get enough sleep. Don’t be afraid to ask gymbros if you’re not sure how to do something. And if something actually truly hurts STOP what you’re doing-your form is likely off or you’re trying to lift too much weight. People are super susceptible to injuries when they first start lifting because they try to push their bodies too fast.

Lastly, take before and after shots-you’ll be pleased in a few weeks when you start seeing results!

Too add to this, watch a lot, and I mean a lot, of good form videos on YouTube. Find good YouTubers that have good form and watch them. Too many times I'm at the gym and see gymbros not having good form and half repping everything.

For example, lat raises. If you go above your shoulder, then you are using your traps. Now it's not a shoulder exercise anymore. Try not to rock or use your body to move the weight.

Another example, incline dumbbell chest press. I see bros all the time doing too much weight and only moving it a few inches. Wtf is that gonna do for you. Make sure you do the complete motion. No half reps, no half motions.

In all movements, go slow and controlled. Feel the full contraction in the right muscles for the movements. If you feel like you are using accessory muscles, check your form and remove some weight if needed.

Watch. Your. Form. More quick examples: Do not drop your elbows in rear delt pulls. For dumbbell rows, try to focus on the back muscles pulling the weight, not relying on the contraction of your bicep to lift the weight. There are multiple ways to squat and deadlift, pick the one that is right for your body type. Etc.

There is a lot to learn, but with diligence and time, you'll be able to be more confident in your lifts to add more weight.

I'm Australian so the coloquialisms go on and on. Most of them, in my opinion, stem from the Australian accent being very lazy. The way to do an Aussie accent is to attempt to speak without opening your mouth so the flies can't get in. This leads to us slurring words together. I have always disliked it and I try to enunciate properly. For example, we say 'Straya instead of Australia," " 'scarnon" instead of "What is going on," and "yeahwegunna" instead of "Yeah, we are going to," and obviously things like g'day, struth, and too right. Most of our speech is in protest of syllables. Anything with 3 or more tends to be chopped and given a nickname. Another thing I missed before was cookies. We don't say cookies, we say biscuits or bickies. Americans say elevator while we say lift and Americans say president while we say fucking cunt.

Actually cunt is an interesting one. Typically anyone is your mate, but it's common to call someone you don't like mate and someone you do a cunt. It's very contextual and not something foreigners do with any success. Don't ever try it if you visit. If I were to be serious with someone, I would say, "Mate, listen ... " whereas madcunt or topcunt can be complimentary and if I was greeting a very close friend, I might address them simply as cunt. Most conversations end with "cheers, mate" or "no worries, mate."

Another one is "yeah, nah." When answering a question, you will often say, "Yeah, nah, I don't know/think so." You do this more often when answering in the negative, but it's possible to say "Yeah, nah, alright." That's weird. It's almost like we toss a coin before deciding whether to answer yes or no.

Last one for now is that when we answer questions, we often tell you half the story and expect you to extrapolate the rest. We don't say "It's hot," we say "It's not cold." We don't tell you we're feeling sick (or crook), we will say we're not feeling great. We don't say "it's big," we say "it's not small." We are ever mysterious.

Obviously most of this stuff is more common the further you get from cities. I am one of the few people I know who actually says g'day regularly.
